title: Video-codec P-frames: delta-encoded memory pages against reference pages
idea: Borrowed from MPEG inter-frame coding: a CXL memory-expander controller keeps 'I-pages' as references and stores near-duplicate pages (VM clones, forked workers, fine-tuned weight variants, beam-search KV copies) as XOR/byte-delta 'P-pages' with offset hints, decoded in a ~20 ns pipeline on read. A MinHash similarity index chooses each page's reference at write-back time.
why: Capacity/cost per bit: near-duplicate (not identical) pages are invisible to exact dedup; claims 2-6x effective capacity on multi-tenant and multi-variant model hosts.

title: Speech-codec linear prediction stores KV cache as residuals
idea: Borrowed from LPC/CELP voice codecs: a tiny per-head linear predictor estimates layer L's keys/values from layer L-1 and the previous token, and only the 1-2 bit quantized prediction residual is stored; predictor coefficients are an offline-fitted codebook. The attention kernel recomputes prediction plus residual on read.
why: KV cache dominates inference DRAM; exploiting cross-layer/cross-token redundancy like speech's formant structure could give 4-8x over 16-bit KV, beyond plain quantization.

title: Airline fare classes and overbooking for server DRAM
idea: Borrowed from airline revenue management: the hypervisor sells each host's DRAM in fare classes (guaranteed, flexible, standby) and overbooks by a learned 'no-show' rate of allocated-but-untouched pages; bumped tenants are migrated to a compressed/CXL tier and credited automatically. An EMSR-style booking-limit algorithm resets per-class caps hourly.
why: Fleet DRAM is often 30-50% allocated-but-idle; yield management turns that slack into 1.3-1.6x sellable capacity without new wafers.

title: Warehouse cross-docking: I/O buffers skip DRAM, land in cache
idea: Borrowed from cross-dock logistics where pallets go straight from inbound to outbound trucks: NIC and NVMe DMA writes are steered into reserved LLC/accelerator-SRAM 'dock doors' with a scheduled consumer appointment, and the consumer's completion frees the door; only overflow spills to DRAM. A hardware yard scheduler enforces the appointment windows.
why: Network/storage staging buffers take GBs per server and double DRAM traffic; removing the staging copy cuts buffer DRAM 80-90% and saves ~2 DRAM passes per byte.

title: Game procedural generation: regenerate pseudorandom tensors from seeds
idea: Borrowed from seed-generated game worlds: any tensor that is pseudorandom by construction (random-feature projections, frozen random bases, sketch hash tables, dropout masks) is stored as a 64-bit seed and regenerated on demand by a counter-based Philox unit beside the tensor core. Models are trained with seeded frozen bases so only small learned coefficients are stored.
why: Turns GBs of stored randomness into bytes; for seeded-basis models, claims 5-20x less weight DRAM at the cost of cheap on-die generation.

title: Vector fonts replace bitmaps: neural hash fields for embedding tables
idea: Borrowed from type foundries' switch from bitmap to outline fonts: recommendation and vocabulary embedding tables (100 GB-10 TB) are replaced by a multi-resolution hash grid plus a tiny MLP decoder (Instant-NGP style) that renders an ID's embedding on demand, with hot IDs memoized in a small cache.
why: Embedding tables are the largest DRAM consumers in ad/recommendation fleets; 10-100x capacity reduction by trading capacity for cheap FLOPs.

title: Freeze-dried heap: dehydrate cold objects, rehydrate on touch
idea: Borrowed from freeze-drying food: the garbage collector moves objects untouched for N cycles into a 'dehydrated' arena where pointers become 24-bit arena-relative varints, headers are dropped and fields are entropy-coded; a load barrier rehydrates an object into the live heap on first access.
why: Managed-language heaps (Java, Python, JS) are 50-70% cold and pointer-bloated; 2-4x footprint reduction on the cold majority.

title: Halftone error diffusion: 2-3-bit stored activations preserving dot products
idea: Borrowed from Floyd-Steinberg print halftoning: when activations or KV are written to memory at 2-3 bits, each element's rounding error is diffused into its not-yet-quantized neighbors along the reduction dimension, so downstream dot products stay nearly unbiased. A small write-path unit performs the diffusion in the store stream.
why: 5-8x fewer bits than FP16 for stored intermediates with accuracy closer to naive 4-6-bit quantization; direct capacity and bandwidth gain.

title: CERN two-level trigger decides which KV entries survive
idea: Borrowed from LHC trigger systems that keep ~1 event in 100,000: new KV entries wait in a fixed-latency level-1 SRAM ring while on-die accumulators sum the attention mass each token receives over the next K steps; only tokens passing the L1 threshold are promoted to DRAM, and a slower software 'high-level trigger' periodically re-scores and drops survivors.
why: Long-context KV grows linearly with tokens; physics-style triggering can keep 5-20% of tokens at small accuracy loss, a 5-20x KV reduction.

title: Backup-appliance dedup at cache-line granularity inside CXL expanders
idea: Borrowed from backup-appliance deduplication: the CXL expander hashes each 64-B line on write, keeps the hash in spare ECC/metadata bits, and maps identical lines to one physical copy through a reference-counted translation table; writes to shared lines trigger copy-on-write inside the controller.
why: Page-level dedup misses intra-page duplication; line-level catches repeated structs, zeros and tenant-shared weights for 1.3-2x capacity on typical cloud memory.

title: Kiva-style robots shuttle memory sleds between racks on demand
idea: Borrowed from warehouse robots that bring shelves to pickers: 1-4 TB CXL memory sleds are hot-pluggable at the top of each rack, and aisle robots physically relocate sleds overnight or within minutes to racks whose forecast demand exceeds supply, steered by a cluster-wide memory demand forecaster.
why: Datacenters provision every rack for its own peak; making memory physically mobile lets the fleet buy for average demand, cutting purchased DRAM 15-30%.

title: Ride-hail surge pricing for an intra-cluster DRAM spot market
idea: Borrowed from surge pricing: the cluster scheduler publishes a real-time internal price per GB-second of DRAM per rack; frameworks (Spark, LLM servers, JVMs) subscribe and automatically switch to compressed formats, smaller caches or quantized KV when the price spikes, with costs charged to team budgets.
why: Exposes DRAM scarcity to software that treats it as free; fleets that price scarce resources typically cut demand 15-30%.

title: Sleep consolidation: idle-time compression of agent memory into gist tokens
idea: Borrowed from hippocampal sleep replay and spaced repetition: when an agent session idles, a background pass replays older context through the model to distill each chunk into a few learned gist tokens, keeping full-fidelity KV only for items retrieved repeatedly (high recall strength) and dropping the rest.
why: Long-lived agent contexts are mostly parked KV; consolidation claims 10-50x less resident KV for idle sessions.

title: Mobile-OS saved-instance-state: kernel discards rebuildable caches by cost
idea: Borrowed from Android, which kills background apps after they save compact state bundles: applications tag regions with a rebuild cost (ns/byte to recompute or re-fetch), and the kernel reclaims the lowest cost-per-byte regions first, signalling the app to rebuild lazily instead of swapping.
why: Caches (memoization, decompressed assets, JIT code) are 20-40% of server RAM; cost-aware discard can shrink provisioned DRAM 15-25% with predictable tails.

title: Scalable-video bit-planes: shed least-significant planes under memory pressure
idea: Borrowed from scalable video coding, where enhancement layers are dropped on congestion: tensors are stored bit-plane-major (MSB plane first), so the memory manager frees LSB planes in place when pressure rises, degrading precision gracefully without re-encoding; reads fetch only the planes that remain.
why: Makes capacity an elastic knob: a server absorbs 1.5-2x demand spikes by dropping planes instead of over-provisioning for peak.

title: Air-freight belly cargo: harvest stranded memory inside peripherals
idea: Borrowed from airlines selling spare cargo space under passenger cabins: idle DRAM in SmartNICs, DPUs, SSD controllers, BMCs and HBM on under-used inference cards is exported as a unified low-priority tier over PCIe/CXL, with a broker that preempts it when the device needs it back.
why: Peripheral DRAM can be 10-30% of a server's total and is mostly idle; harvesting it cuts host DIMM purchases by a similar fraction.

title: Printing-press plates: one copy of model weights serves many hosts
idea: Borrowed from printing, where one plate prints a whole run: a CXL 3.x multi-host shared-memory appliance holds a single read-only copy of popular model weights mapped into 8-32 servers, each of which keeps only KV and activations locally; a hot-row SRAM cache in the switch absorbs repeated reads.
why: Every inference host now stores its own copy of the same 100-800 GB of weights; sharing cuts weight DRAM 8-32x across a pod.

title: Postal ZIP codes: region-relative 32-bit pointers in hardware
idea: Borrowed from postal routing (zone plus local address): an ISA extension where pointers are 32-bit 'ZIP + offset' values resolved through a region register file in the load unit, letting native data structures use half-size pointers, not just JVM compressed oops.
why: Pointer-heavy data (graphs, trees, object heaps) is 30-50% pointers; 20-35% footprint reduction across native code.

title: VoIP silence suppression: never store zero or constant lines
idea: Borrowed from VoIP, which sends a tiny comfort-noise descriptor instead of silence: the memory controller keeps a per-page bitmap of zero or single-value 64-B lines, allocates no DRAM for them and synthesizes them on read, compacting the remaining lines into a smaller frame.
why: Sparse activations, fresh allocations and padded tensors are often 20-60% zero/constant lines; that capacity and bandwidth is reclaimed.

title: Seismic stacking: memory-side reduce-on-write for accumulation buffers
idea: Borrowed from seismic and astronomical co-adding, where traces are summed on arrival instead of stored: memory expanders implement vector add-on-write (FP32/BF16), so N producers (gradient buckets, histograms, embedding-gradient scatters) accumulate into one shared buffer instead of each holding a private copy for a later reduction.
why: Removes N-1 copies of accumulation buffers; 2-8x less DRAM for reduction-heavy workloads.

title: JPEG for KV: DCT along the sequence axis, keep low frequencies
idea: Borrowed from JPEG: blocks of 64 consecutive tokens' keys/values per head are DCT-transformed along the token axis and only significant coefficients are stored with zig-zag run-length coding; attention for old blocks is computed directly in the frequency domain.
why: Adjacent tokens' KV are strongly correlated in many heads; 4-10x compression of older context with error confined to high-frequency detail.

title: Retail UPC registry: global value interning in the memory controller
idea: Borrowed from UPC barcodes, where one global registry gives each product a short code: the memory controller learns a table of the ~4K most frequent 64-bit values (pointer prefixes, enum constants, common floats) and stores them as 12-bit codes inside a compressed line format shared across all processes.
why: Value locality in real heaps is high; 1.3-1.8x effective capacity, complementary to zero elision and dedup.

title: Satellite downlink budgets: storage-side filtering before data reaches DRAM
idea: Borrowed from Earth-observation satellites that process onboard because downlink is scarce: each query gets a 'downlink budget' in host DRAM bytes, and the planner pushes filters, projections and pre-aggregation into computational SSDs until the result fits, so raw scans never land in DRAM.
why: Analytics engines buffer raw columnar data in DRAM; pushing selection into storage cuts working-set DRAM 5-20x for selective queries.

title: Cold-chain use-by dates: TTL-typed memory in refresh-free banks
idea: Borrowed from perishable-food logistics where every pallet carries a use-by date: allocations carry a time-to-live (malloc_ttl, compiler-known tensor lifetimes), and the controller places sub-retention lifetimes in banks with refresh permanently disabled, built with ~5x smaller capacitors that only need ~10 ms retention; long-lived data goes to SRAM or non-volatile tiers.
why: Zero refresh power for the ephemeral majority (activations, request heaps, packet buffers); small-capacitor ephemeral cells sidestep the 60-75:1 charge wall for denser, cheaper bits.

title: Street-sweeper routes: LLM weight reads double as refresh
idea: Borrowed from municipal sweeper routes that cover every street on a fixed cycle: during decode every weight row is read once per token (~10-30 ms), so the controller orders weight fetches as a route covering every row inside the retention window and disables explicit refresh for weight banks; when the server idles the banks may decay and are reloaded from flash on wake.
why: Weights are the largest DRAM region on inference servers; zero refresh power and 10-20% bandwidth recovered, so fewer or smaller stacks deliver the same throughput.

title: Grocery spoil-and-restock: refresh-free DRAM as clean-only cache
idea: Borrowed from produce departments that discard spoiled stock and restock from the warehouse: DRAM runs with refresh off and holds only clean copies whose master lives in CXL or flash; each row has weak 'canary' cells plus a CRC, a read that finds a tripped canary simply re-fetches, and dirty data stays in a small SRAM write buffer that writes through.
why: Zero refresh energy and 10-20% bandwidth back; the DRAM tier shrinks to a pure cache, and cells no longer need to meet the 64 ms tail spec, improving yield and cost.

title: Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: KV cache that evicts by natural decay
idea: Borrowed from human memory, where recall strengthens traces and neglect lets them fade: KV entries live in refresh-free DRAM where every attention read restores the row's charge, so attended tokens persist and ignored tokens decay; a per-row parity bit flags decayed entries, which attention masks out as forgotten.
why: Both the eviction policy and refresh disappear: zero refresh power, and the KV footprint self-limits to the actively attended set (often 10-30% of tokens).

title: Fiber-optic Z-channel codes stretch unrefreshed retention to minutes
idea: Borrowed from asymmetric-channel coding in optical links: since leakage only flips charged cells to discharged (a Z-channel), data are inverted/encoded so ~90% of cells rest in the non-leaking state and protected with cheap unidirectional-error-correcting (Berger/Bose-Lin) codes; with the weak-cell tail corrected, the safe unrefreshed window grows from 64 ms toward minutes, long enough for natural rewrites or discard to cover all data.
why: Makes refresh-off operation practical for most data classes (zero refresh power) and lowers per-bit write energy by keeping most cells uncharged.

title: Wine-cellar racking: match data lifetime to each row's retention
idea: Borrowed from cellars that put long-aging vintages in the coolest, most stable racks: a boot-time and online profiler bins every row by measured retention (most rows hold 1-10 s, only a tail is near 64 ms), and the OS places each page by its predicted rewrite interval into a row that outlasts it; pages with uncertain lifetimes go to a non-volatile shelf.
why: Removes refresh by exploiting the retention distribution instead of designing for the 13 fA tail; recovers 16-33% of idle power and keeps weak-retention dies in service, raising usable supply.

title: Vinyl-record pressing: via-programmed mask ROM for frozen model weights
idea: Borrowed from record pressing, where one stamper makes millions of discs: frozen model weights are pressed into 1-transistor mask ROM by a single cheap via/metal mask on a commodity logic wafer (no EUV, no capacitor) stacked under the accelerator, so weights need zero DRAM and zero refresh; a new model version is a new via mask.
why: Removes the weight footprint from DRAM; mask ROM is dense, has zero standby and refresh power, uses mature U.S.-available nodes and needs no capacitor or EUV.

title: Pre-printed forms: frozen base weights, only adapters live in SRAM
idea: Borrowed from pre-printed forms where only the handwritten fields vary: models are split into a frozen base held in non-volatile storage and per-tenant low-rank adapters plus normalization deltas (a few MB each) held in on-die SRAM; the scheduler batches requests by adapter so mutable state never exceeds SRAM.
why: Multi-tenant fine-tune serving needs no DRAM for per-tenant weights and no refresh; 100+ tenants per accelerator instead of one full copy each.

title: Player-piano rolls: stream weights from NAND page buffers to compute
idea: Borrowed from player pianos reading music straight off a moving roll: NAND dies with wide internal page buffers stream compressed weights over a short die-to-die bus directly into the NPU's SRAM line buffers, with dozens of planes interleaved so the read rate matches decode throughput and no DRAM staging exists.
why: Weights sit in NAND at ~1/10 the cost per bit of DRAM with zero refresh; DRAM shrinks to KV/activations, cutting capacity per inference server 5-10x.

title: Restaurant cook-to-order: store token IDs, recompute KV on demand
idea: Borrowed from kitchens that cook to order instead of holding a buffet: long contexts are kept as token IDs (2 bytes/token) and the KV for any needed span is re-prefilled in compute-dense bursts into SRAM tiles just before attention, with only a small recent window kept resident.
why: At rest, per-token state drops from ~100 KB-1 MB of KV to 2 bytes; no long-lived volatile state means nothing to refresh, trading spare FLOPs for capacity.

title: Utility meters, not itemized bills: fixed-size recurrent state in SRAM
idea: Borrowed from utility meters that keep a running total instead of every transaction: most attention layers are replaced by fixed-size recurrent/state-space states (a few MB per sequence) held in SRAM, plus a few exact-attention layers over a short local window.
why: Removes the linearly growing KV cache from DRAM; per-sequence memory becomes constant and fits on-die, so refresh power is zero.

title: Double-entry ledgers: derive state from an append-only NVM journal
idea: Borrowed from accounting, where balances are derived from an immutable journal: services keep only an append-only event log in non-volatile memory and compute derived views (indexes, aggregates, session state) on demand into SRAM scratch, caching only results whose reuse distance is under a millisecond.
why: Eliminates large DRAM-resident materialized views and session caches in transactional systems; no long-lived volatile state, so zero refresh power.

title: Dairy fresh-processing: consume activations in-DRAM before they decay
idea: Borrowed from dairies that process milk within hours rather than store it: activations are written into refresh-free DRAM subarrays and consumed within microseconds by charge-sharing multiply-accumulate in the same subarray (processing-in-memory), so no datum ever has to outlive milliseconds.
why: Combines compute-in-memory with ephemerality: zero refresh power, 3-20 pJ/bit of host data movement avoided, and capacitors sized for microseconds rather than 64 ms.

title: Toyota kanban: WIP tokens keep fused-operator intermediates on-chip
idea: Borrowed from kanban cards that cap work-in-progress between stations: a dataflow accelerator passes hardware kanban tokens between fused operator stages, and a producer may emit a tile only when its consumer returns a token, bounding every intermediate tensor to a fixed SRAM budget so activations never touch DRAM.
why: Intermediates (often 30-60% of inference/training DRAM capacity and traffic) stay in SRAM with zero refresh; DRAM need shrinks to weights and checkpoints.

title: Hong Kong high-rises: 8-high hybrid-bonded SRAM as sole memory
idea: Borrowed from dense cities that build upward when land is scarce: eight thinned, capacitor-free SRAM dies on a mature node are hybrid-bonded onto an edge inference SoC for 0.5-1 GB of sub-5 ns on-package SRAM, and 2-bit weights let small models and their KV fit entirely, removing DRAM from the bill of materials.
why: Zero refresh and zero DRAM purchase for edge devices; stacking mature-node SRAM avoids EUV and the HBM TSV yield tax.

title: Library card catalogs: SRAM filters front non-volatile records
idea: Borrowed from libraries that keep a compact card catalog by the door and books in the stacks: large DRAM hash tables (dedup indexes, key-value stores, routing tables) are replaced by SRAM-resident ribbon/cuckoo filters plus learned position models that point to the exact NVM block, so each lookup costs one NVM read.
why: Index structures often dominate server DRAM; filters need ~1-2 bytes per key versus 30-100 in DRAM tables, a 20-50x reduction with no refresh.

title: Holography: superpose thousands of associations in one SRAM hypervector
idea: Borrowed from holograms, where many images share one plate: older KV pairs are bound (permute-multiply or circular convolution) and summed into a fixed set of high-dimensional superposition vectors in SRAM, and attention queries unbind from them, with a small cleanup memory for exact recall of key items.
why: Bounded memory for unbounded context: a growing DRAM KV becomes fixed SRAM with zero refresh; the capacity-versus-noise trade-off is the risk.

title: Day-old bakery pricing: discounted refresh-free 'ephemeral RAM' cloud tier
idea: Borrowed from bakeries selling day-old bread at a discount: a cloud instance class offers memory guaranteed only ~1 s without access (hardware refresh off), surfaced through a 'spoiled page' signal like SIGBUS; stream processors, inference servers and caches opt in at ~40% lower price per GB.
why: Creates a market that funds refresh-free hardware and moves ephemeral workloads off full-spec DRAM; dies that fail the 64 ms bin become sellable, raising effective supply.

title: Audio mastering dither: retention decay as free training noise
idea: Borrowed from audio mastering, where deliberate dither noise improves perceived quality: activations saved for backprop live in refresh-free DRAM, with sign/exponent bits stored in the non-leaking state so only mantissa LSBs can decay, and the sparse bit flips that accrue before the backward pass act as stochastic-rounding/dropout-like noise.
why: Zero refresh for training's largest memory consumer, and decay tolerance admits denser weak-retention cells; could be accuracy-neutral or even regularizing.

title: Bear hibernation: migrate idle rows to NVM before retention expires
idea: Borrowed from hibernating animals that drop to near-zero metabolism: the controller timestamps each row's last activation and, when an untouched row nears its retention deadline, moves it once into a dense non-volatile tier and marks it hibernating instead of refreshing it; a later access wakes it back into DRAM.
why: Periodic refresh becomes a one-time migration of cold rows; DRAM holds only the awake working set (often 20-40% of allocated), shrinking provisioned DRAM with zero refresh power.

title: Teletext data carousel: broadcast weights to accelerators that store nothing
idea: Borrowed from broadcast TV data carousels that loop content for any receiver to catch: a rack-level weight server streams the model layer by layer in a continuous optical multicast loop from ROM/NAND, and every accelerator computes on each layer as it passes, aligning its batches to the carousel phase.
why: N accelerators share one non-volatile copy of weights with zero weight DRAM and zero refresh; per-accelerator DRAM shrinks to KV only.

title: Court-stenographer chords: bigger tokens shrink KV until it fits SRAM
idea: Borrowed from stenotype machines that write whole words in one chord: the model uses latent multi-byte patch tokens (dynamic 8-16-byte patches) so each KV entry covers ~4x more text, and with latent low-rank KV projection a 32k-character context fits in on-die SRAM.
why: About 4x fewer KV entries times 4-8x smaller entries gives 16-32x less KV memory, small enough to live in SRAM with zero refresh.

title: Appliance energy labels: 'R0 zero-refresh' procurement class for memory
idea: Borrowed from ENERGY STAR and EU appliance labels: U.S. federal and CHIPS-funded datacenter procurement adopts an 'R0' rating for servers whose memory hierarchy spends no power on refresh (SRAM, ROM, NVM or refresh-free ephemeral tiers), with a 10-15% price preference and published watts per idle GB.
why: Creates a guaranteed early market for refresh-free, less-DRAM architectures; refresh is 16-33% of idle memory power across the fleet it targets.
